reviewer: Codex source-guided review; not independent human annotation
scope: All 109 supported broader-sample cases and all 15 supported concept cases with different IE-CoR expert sets. Other supported concept cases remain pending.
open_notes_in_packet_order: Both sources trace the terms through Late Latin metonymia and Greek metonymia. Shared source is supported; the specialist definition mismatch remains unresolved.
Both descend from recorded snithana; the Danish entry is historical. Historical relation does not establish current interchangeable uses.
Both record Germanic skalo. Shell overlap is supported; broad source relation leaves transmission unspecified.
Both record Germanic nu. Noun moment and modal particle are distinct displayed uses despite related entries.
Both record Germanic kruppaz. Torso and goitre displays remain distinct meanings.
Both record Germanic gans. The Danish prose explicitly names Dutch gans; goose scope differs across the inventories.

The Dutch source explicitly compares Danish nabo. These independently formed near/inhabitant compounds support a related family; a cognate mention alone does not prove inheritance of the complete compound.
Both record Germanic obijana; Dutch oefenen is an iterative formation. Shared source is supported without claiming unchanged whole-word formation.
Both sources record French billet borrowing. The loan relationship is supported and kept separate from native inherited cognacy.
Both inherit West Germanic sterno. Star history is supported independently of the inventories' other meanings.
Both explicitly borrow Latin spatium. Duplicate paths are repeated evidence, not independent confirmation.
Both trace to Latin statura. Shared source is supported; the templates do not specify the complete transmission route.
Both record Germanic skapa. Chest and historical shape displays are not a modern equivalent pair.
Dutch bird frater is likely onomatopoeic; Latin frater is only a suggested alternative. The shared-Latin path is qualified, not established. The extractor failed to retain this prose qualification.
Both trace to Latin legio, with French transmission on the Dutch side. This supports shared source rather than purely native inheritance.
Both record Germanic felgo and German explicitly names Dutch velg. Wheel-rim history is supported.
Dutch jol is only possibly from Low German jolle; the deeper Indo-European route is also possible. Both recovered paths need these qualifications; the current extractor omits them.
Both record Germanic warton and explicit cross-language mentions. One German mention gloss says to grow, but the independent shared ancestor supports the noun pair.

The complete Germanic tugilaz word and explicit Dutch cognate mention support the relation. The broad component flag is overly conservative because a same-language suffix analysis also appears; it does not invalidate the explicit statement.
Shared West Germanic hreud and explicit riet mention are supported. English says the further origin is uncertain; this qualifies deeper origin, not the recorded West Germanic comparison.
Both record Latin pastinaca. The English form underwent additional French and English reshaping; shared source is supported without asserting identical formation.
Shared Middle Dutch hoppe and Germanic huppo are supported. The deeper Indo-European origin is only possible and must remain qualified.
Both trace to Greek haimatites. The source describes the complete mineral name, not merely a shared blood component.

English borrows Latin fabrica; Dutch offers Latin fabrica or French fabrique. Shared Latin source is plausible, but direct Dutch borrowing from Latin is an alternative route, not uniquely established.
Both explicitly borrow Italian tiramisu. The shared borrowing path is supported.
Both trace the verbs to Germanic dukana and explicitly compare duck/duiken. Displayed head-lowering and diving uses still require the separate meaning assessment.
Both record West Germanic sikilu and an explicit cognate statement. The common form itself was an early Latin borrowing; the relation is not proof of purely native Germanic origin.
Both record West Germanic awi and Germanic awiz, with explicit cross-language mentions. The ewe relationship is supported.
Both record West Germanic gelu and Germanic gelwaz. The shared color entry is supported; supplemental comparisons to other colors do not change this pair.
Both trace to French huguenot. The English prose qualifies its further origin as uncertain, not the French source correspondence.
Dutch explicitly borrows English panorama. The direct whole-word path is supported; the English Greek-component formation is a separate fact.
Both trace to Latin permissio. Leave of absence and permission are related but not the same displayed use.

The shared wesana verb is supported. Dutch noun wezen is explicitly a substantivization; Norwegian has suppletive present forms. This is a derived family relation, not proof that every inflected form shares one root.
Both record Germanic hrugnaz. The roe comparison is supported within its regional and usage limits.
Both record Latin Ceres, but the displayed goddess and Dutch neighborhood are different entities. Shared name history does not establish entity identity.
Both trace to Latin tendere; Norwegian passes through German. Verb and tendency noun remain different formations and parts of speech.
Both explicitly borrow French telegraphie. Same-language surface analyses do not invalidate the common complete loan.
Both record Germanic fodijana and an explicit voeden mention. Birth and feeding displays are distinct despite the related entries.
Both record Germanic gans. Goose history is supported; the Dutch definition has broader stated scope.
Both record Germanic bulstraz. Bur and pillow are distinct displayed meanings of historically related words.
Both record Germanic tigulon. Dutch further records Latin tegula; inherited common early loan and ultimate borrowing are compatible facts.
Both record Germanic uns. Objective pronoun history is supported without claiming complete inventory equivalence.
Both record Germanic swester. The Dutch prose specifically explains the sister-to-nurse development; the selected nurse senses do not invalidate the historical relation.
Both record Germanic gans. Swedish prose qualifies the other senses as developments from goose flotation; that does not change the goose relationship.
Both record Germanic nu. Modal particle and noun moment are different uses; a shared ancestor does not make these displays equivalent.
Both record Germanic hawwana. Hewing and forcefully grabbing displays are different uses of related entries.
Both record Germanic warton. The Dutch irregular sound development is explicitly discussed, not evidence against the documented relation.

Both record the complete Germanic handuwerka and an explicit cognate mention. Additional hand/work formation claims cause an overly broad component flag; they do not make the complete ancestor a component-only match.

Icelandic smali develops through livestock and a shortened herdsman compound from the small adjective. The broad shared smalaz source supports a derivational family, not inherited equivalence of whole words.
Both record Low German schinke borrowing. Deeper shared forms are supported; the Icelandic tanning use remains a separate semantic development.

Shared Old Norse hinn is supported. Danish prose explicitly calls Germanic jainaz phonologically distinct; the extracted shared jainaz path is mis-scoped and must be excluded without discarding the valid hinn path.
Icelandic explicitly records Danish porre borrowing. Latin porrum is also recorded on both sides; the direct borrowing remains supported.
Both trace to Greek amoibe. Icelandic borrows Danish amoba, a different spelling from the row's amobe, so this run does not establish a direct resolved row-to-row borrowing path.
Both record Old Norse ar and Germanic airo for oar. The selected etymology entries match this meaning.
Both record Old Norse elfr and Germanic albi; Danish is borrowed from Norwegian. Shared source is supported, with the borrowing route preserved in prose.
Both record Old Norse reynir. Danish also relates the form to red; the complete reynir correspondence is supported.
The Icelandic interrogative is explicitly a neuter formation and conflation involving hwaz. Shared source supports a grammatical family; who and adverbial how are not equivalent forms.
Both record Old Norse hlemmr and Germanic hlammiz. Lid/trapdoor scope remains a separate meaning distinction.
Both inherit Old Norse ungi. Its older adjectival derivation does not invalidate the shared complete noun.
Both explicitly borrow French estragon. Shared loan history is supported.
German prose explicitly compares Icelandic loft in the air word's history. The statement supports the selected noun entries.
Both record Germanic flatja. Large hearth room and bunk remain different displayed meanings.
Both record Germanic gata, with Low German borrowing on the German side. The broad relation does not assert purely native inheritance on both sides.
Both record Germanic glodiz and an explicit Icelandic cognate mention. Heat and embers scope is separately reviewed.
Both record Germanic magraz and Indo-European mh2kros. Common forms support the relation without implying full overlap of skinny/thin uses.
Both trace to Latin Maurus. This is a shared historical source, not evidence of independent native Germanic inheritance.
Both record Germanic finhlo. Different intermediary forms are documented; broad shared-source evidence is supported.
Both record Germanic meduz and Indo-European medhu. Common mead source is supported, independently of further honey comparisons.
Both record Germanic theubaz. Thief entry history is supported.
Both trace to Latin massa, but massif has a French adjectival route and massi is a mass noun. Shared source supports related formations rather than inherited whole-word identity.

Both record Old English sape and Germanic saipon, with an explicit Icelandic mention. The source does not establish the precise transmission of Old English into Icelandic; the deeper Indo-European route is additionally uncertain in the tree.
Both record Latin benedictus, one as an archaic adjective and one through a name. Shared source does not establish current meaning overlap or generic personal-name identity.
Both record the complete Germanic uwwulon owl form. Earlier imitative or alternative origin remains qualified; it does not invalidate that common intermediate form.
Both record Germanic langaz and Indo-European dlonghos. English duration and Icelandic height are distinct selected uses despite the shared entry history.
Both record Germanic menoths and an explicit Icelandic cognate mention. Further moon/measure derivation is qualified and is not needed for the supported month relation.
Both record Old Norse angra. Bothering and regretting are related meanings, not interchangeable displays.
Both record Old Norse greida and Germanic garaidijana. Paying and being able are distinct current displays.
Both record the complete Old Norse groftr. Additional suffix decomposition caused the broad component flag; the whole-word Old Norse inheritance path is independently supported.
Both record Old Norse flesk and an explicit Icelandic mention. Norwegian qualifies the further origin as uncertain; keep that deeper uncertainty separate from the common Norse word.
Both record Old Norse kne and Germanic knewa. Knee history is supported; repeated paths are not independent evidence.
Both name entries trace to Old Norse Sindri. This supports related name forms but does not resolve the earlier generic-name meaning judgment or identify a particular person.
Both record Old Norse daufr and Germanic daubaz, with Danish transmission on the Norwegian side. Pallid and deaf displays remain distinct and the recorded overlap is historical.
The Norwegian source explicitly names Icelandic Eyrarsund and both displays identify the same strait. Component analyses coexist with a supported whole-name correspondence.

Shared Old Norse aboti is supported. Old English transmission is described as likely and variant-dependent, so the deeper shared-source paths need that qualification; do not reject the common Norse form.
Both record Old Norse therna for the tern. The whole-word source correspondence is supported.
Both record Old Norse mik. Reflexive myself and objective me are grammatical variants with distinct displayed uses.
Both trace to Greek amoibe. Icelandic additionally gives Danish transmission; broad source evidence does not uniquely settle the complete Norwegian route.
Both record Germanic finhlo. Shared file-tool source is supported despite differing documented intermediaries.
Both record Germanic kubo. The boat and shanty meanings require the saved specialist review; shared source does not resolve that semantic uncertainty.
Both record Germanic listiz. Skill and cunning plan are related but not equivalent displayed uses.
Both record Germanic thinga. Assembly/parliament and thing are historically related; current meaning overlap is a separate restricted/historical issue.
Both record Germanic warton. Shared wart history is supported despite the documented irregular Dutch development.
Both record Germanic wintruz. Winter source is supported; regional inventory differences remain separate.
Both record Germanic witana. The source also gives different deeper forms of the same root; exact deepest-root spelling is unnecessary for this relation.
Both record Germanic batizo. Comparative and generic high-quality displays remain different grammatical scope; common source does not justify equivalence of displayed definitions.
Both record Germanic daubaz. Pallid/deaf selected meanings remain distinct; historical overlap does not settle current label correctness.
Both record Germanic draumijana. Icelandic experiencer syntax is explicitly described; the syntactic difference does not invalidate the historical word comparison.
Shared hwaz supports an interrogative family through Icelandic neuter formation and conflation. How and who are different forms and displayed meanings.
Both record Old Norse greip and Germanic graipo, with an explicit Swedish comparison in Icelandic prose. Grasp/tool meanings are related, not equivalent displays.

The common Old Norse skata and cross-language mentions are supported for ray and magpie developments. Deeper skade derivation is speculative; preserve this qualification on the broad path rather than rejecting the common Norse word.
Both record Old Norse digr and Germanic digraz. Shared stout/thick source is supported with separately assessed current scope.
Both record Old Norse rjupa. The ptarmigan comparison is supported; species and generic scope remain separate.
Both record Old Norse ofund and Germanic abundiz. Envy history is supported.
Both place-name entries record Old Norse Skaney and Germanic Skadinawjo and identify the same region. This supports the name comparison, not a general personal-name matching rule.
Both record Old Norse daufr and Germanic daubaz. Pallid/deaf displays remain different; recorded historical overlap is not current synonymy.

Both record Old Norse nahvalr, but the Icelandic compound derivation and Swedish metathesis route are qualified as probable. Retain those qualifications rather than presenting an unqualified complete transmission.
Shared hwaz supports a grammatical family through the Icelandic neuter/conflated form. The selected how and who uses are not equivalent.
Both inherit the complete Old Norse laugardagr. The day-name correspondence is supported without inferring every modern cultural use is identical.
Both record Old Norse throstr and an explicit Swedish cognate mention. Deeper forms differ, but the common Norse word supports the thrush comparison.
different_expert_set_notes_in_packet_ord: rund/rond: both trace through French to Latin rotundus. Shared loan source is supported; different expert sets do not refute it.
kort/kort: common West Germanic kurt is recorded, with early Latin borrowing on the Dutch side and Low German transmission into Danish. Different expert sets can reflect borrowing history.
dreje/draaien: explicit cross-language mention and common Germanic/West Germanic sources support the relationship, while Danish records Low German transmission.
rund/rond: shared Latin/French history is supported, but the selected adverb/preposition around meanings do not match the benchmark round adjective.
round/rond: both record Latin rotundus through French. Shared borrowing ancestry is supported without equating expert-set membership.

turn/draaien: shared Indo-European terh1 is a distant root connection through distinct formations and English Latin/French borrowing. It is not proof of inherited whole-word cognacy at the benchmark's level.

cloud/wolk: reject the explicit cognate edge. English prose applies the Dutch wolk mention to displaced welkne/welkin, not cloud. Cloud has klutaz ancestry and wolk has wolkn; their ordinary translation comparison remains valid.
egg/ei: common Germanic ajja is recorded; English egg enters through Norse borrowing and replaces native ey. Different expert sets do not disprove the shared historical source.
kort/kort: both trace to Latin curtus, with Low German/Norse transmission into Norwegian. Shared borrowing history is supported.
rond/rund: both trace through French, with Low German transmission into Swedish. Shared source is supported.
kort/kort: both record West Germanic kurt and Latin curtus; Swedish records Low German transmission. Shared source is supported with borrowing routes retained.

root/rot: English explicitly names Icelandic rot and both record the Norse/Germanic root, with Norse borrowing into English. Selected figurative origin meanings are wrong for the benchmark plant-root concept.
egg/egg: common Norse egg and Germanic ajja are supported; Norse borrowing into English explains why expert-set membership alone is an insufficient negative reference.

bark/borkur: English explicitly names Icelandic borkur and records Norse borrowing. The common Norse and Germanic forms support the relationship; the deeper birch/Indo-European derivation is only probable.

borkur/bark: both record common Norse borkr and Germanic barkuz. Different expert sets do not invalidate this documented correspondence; its transmission detail remains outside what broad derived_from templates establish.
